problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

If $x(t)=t-2{t}^{2}$ and $y(t)=t+k$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
worked_solution:
Since $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-2{t}^{2})(t+k)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(kt+(1-2k){t}^{2}-2{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{k{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{(1-2k){t}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{1-2k}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{k-1}{2}+\frac{1-2k}{3} & =0 \\ 3(k-1)+2(1-2k) & =0 \\ 3k-3+2-4k & =0 \\ -1-k & =0 \\ k & =-1\end{aligned}
$$
